markdown_chunks.section: **Geometric Effects of Liquid Rocket Engine Pintle Injectors** **in Supercritical Combustion** > 1 Introduction
markdown_chunks.text:
Pintle injectors for liquid rocket engines have a single element protruding from the center of the head of combustors.
In pintle injectors, a propellant is injected in the axial direction of a combustion chamber from the annular ring to form
a sheet along the circumference of the pintle post. This propellant collides with another propellant discharged radially
from the tip of the pintle at right angles. The mixed propellants form a cone-shaped spray pattern near the pintle tip.
Therefore, the pintle injector releases energy to the acoustic
node of the combustion chamber and provides high combustion stability. Furthermore, a recirculation zone with a
high OFR formed along the combustion chamber axis at
the tip of the pintle improves the combustion efficiency by
allowing unburned propellant to participate in the combustion again [1, 2].

Since the pintle injector was first proposed by Elverum

[3] in the late 1950s, studies on various subjects on the pintle
injector have continued into the 2000s, mainly by researchers
of TRW Inc. Dressler and Bauer briefly reported the history
of TRW in the research and development of pintle injectors

[4]. The liquid pintle injector studies in TRW revealed that
pintle injectors with discontinuous two-row orifices provide
the highest characteristic velocity efficiency ( _ηC_ <sup>_*_</sup> ), and various geometric parameters can affect combustor performance

Pintle injectors have attracted considerable attention again
after their use in successful spacecraft and reusable launch
vehicle missions. Austin et al. reported that the characteristic velocity efficiency was asymptotically maximized at
a TMR of 0.7 by conducting combustion tests with fuelcentered discontinuous two-row circular pintle orifices using
a non-toxic self-igniting propellant. Furthermore, they studied the characteristic length ( _L_ <sup>_*_</sup> ), pintle-combustion chamber
diameter ratio ( _D_ c/ _D_ p), secondary-to-primary orifice diameter ratio, skip distance ( _L_ S), and pulse mode operation [8].
Bedard et al. fabricated a liquid oxygen-liquid methane pintle injector combustor with a fixed area orifice to achieve
30% throttling [9]. Yu et al. performed single-row squareshaped orifice pintle-combustion tests and confirmed that the
effect of the TMR was qualitatively more dominant than that
of the BF [10]. In a study with the canted slit pintle, Yu
et al. reported that _ηC_ <sup>_*_</sup> converged to a maximum at _L_ <sup>_*_</sup> 0.75 m [11], which is consistent with the study by Austin
et al. [8]. Sakaki et al. observed that ηC <sup>_*_</sup> increased with a

droplet size distribution [18].

As in the literature review, several studies on various pintle injector parameters were performed. However, they were
limited to the water flow test or, as shown in Table 1, the
subcritical condition combustion tests for oxidizers. However, most high-performance liquid rocket engines operate
in supercritical conditions. Supercritical combustion properties differ from subcritical conditions due to the propellant’s
loss of surface tension and high diffusivity [19]. Therefore,
additional research is necessary to extend the understanding of pintle injector operation characteristics at supercritical
conditions. In particular, the pintle injector having a discontinuous orifice has various geometric variables, unlike the
continuous type. In this study, to understand a pintle injector operation characteristic at supercritical conditions [20],
combustion tests were performed on 1.5-tonf class two-row
pintle injectors with discontinuous orifices under a combustion pressure of 70 bar using LOx/Jet A-1 as propellants. This
study focused on the effects of TMR and BF on _ηC_ <sup>_*_</sup> and their
pressure fluctuation characteristics.
